answer.text:
This is the self biased shunt-shunt inverter, Fig 3.14
in Razavi. 

$$\eqalign{
g_{m}&=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\cr
r_{o}&=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\cr
A_{0}&=-g_{m}r_{o}}$$

$$C_{1}\approx {\rm short}$$

$$\eqalign{
G_{m}v_{i}+{{v_{o}-v_{i}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{v_{o}}\over {r_{o}}}=0\cr
{\rm for}\;v_{i}= {\rm input}\;,v_{o}={\rm output}}$$

$$A_{v}\equiv {{v_{o}}\over {v_{i}}}={{1/R_{F}-g_{m}}\over {1/R_{F}+1/r_{o}}}
\approx -g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}\tag{1}$$

With $R_{s}$ at the input

$$\eqalign{
{{v_{i}-v_{s}}\over {R_{s}}}+{{v_{i}-v_{o}}\over {R_{F}}}&=0\cr
-g_{m}v_{i}+{{v_{o}-v_{i}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{v_{o}}\over {r_{o}}}&=0}$$

$$R_{in}\equiv {{v_{i}}\over {i_{in}}}={{v_{i}}\over {(v_{i}-v_{o})/R_{F}}}
={{R_{F}}\over {1-A_{v}}}= {{r_{o}+R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\tag{2}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {{R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\approx 
{{1}\over {g_{m}}}+{{R_{F}}\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}\qquad g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$$

i. e. $R_{in}$ is no longer $R_{F}$ and no longer
$1/g_{m}$. For $R_{F}\gg r_{o}$ $R_{in}\to 1/g_{m}$, for
$R_{F}\ll r_{o}$ $R_{in}\to R_{F}/g_{m}r_{o}$.
Normally $50\Omega $ is obtained with $g_{m}R_{s}\ne 1$.

Let $\overline{i_{n,R_{F}}^{2}}=4kT/R_{F}$ in parallel
with $R_{F}$ and 
$\overline{i_{n,D}^{2}}=4kT\gamma g_{m1}+4kT\gamma g_{m2}
=4kT\gamma g_{m}$ at the output.

Writing nodal equations with $v_{s}$, $i_{n,R_{F}}$, $i_{n,D}$

$$\left[ \matrix{
1/R_{s}+1/R_{F} &-1/R_{F}\cr
g_{m}-1/R_{F} &1/R_{F}+1/r_{o}}\right]
\left[ \matrix{v_{i}\cr v_{o}}\right] =
\left[ \matrix{v_{s}/R_{s}-i_{n,R_{F}}\cr i_{n,R_{F}}-i_{n,D}}\right] $$

$D=(1/R_{s}+1/R_{F})(1/R_{F}+1/r_{o})+(1/R_{F})(g_{m}-1/R_{F})$

$$\eqalign{
v_{o}\vert_{v_{s}}&=-{{g_{m}-1/R_{F}}\over {R_{s}D}}v_{s}\cr
v_{o}\vert_{R_{F}}&={{g_{m}+1/R_{s}}\over {D}}i_{n,R_{F}}\cr
v_{o}\vert_{D}&=-{{1/R_{s}+1/R_{F}}\over {D}}i_{n,D}}$$

$$\eqalign{
S_{vo,R_{s}}&={{(g_{m}-1/R_{F})^{2}}\over {R_{s}^{2}D^{2}}}4kTR_{s}\cr
S_{vo,R_{F}}&={{(g_{m}+1/R_{s})^{2}}\over {D^{2}}}{{4kT}\over {R_{F}}}\cr
S_{vo,D}&={{(1/R_{s}+1/R_{F})^{2}}\over {D^{2}}}4kT\gamma g_{m}}$$

$$F\equiv {{S_{vo,R_{s}}+S_{vo,R_{F}}+S_{vo,D}}\over {S_{vo,R_{s}}}}$$

$$F=1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}
\left({{g_{m}+1/R_{s}}\over {g_{m}-1/R_{F}}}\right)^{2}
+\gamma g_{m}R_{s}
\left({{1/R_{s}+1/R_{F}}\over {g_{m}-1/R_{F}}}\right)^{2}\tag{3}$$

$D$ and $r_{o}$ drop out. For the usual
$g_{m}\gg 1/R_{F},1/R_{s}$

$$F\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}
\left(1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}\right)^{2}
\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\tag{4}$$

and with $\gamma _{1}\ne \gamma_{2}$

$$\gamma g_{m}\to \gamma_{n}g_{m1}+\gamma_{p}g_{m2}\tag{5}$$

$$F\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+
{{\gamma_{n}g_{m1}+\gamma_{p}g_{m2}}\over {g_{m}^{2}R_{s}}}$$

$R_{s}=R_{in}=50\Omega $ when matched.
The familiar $F\approx 1+\gamma$ for
$1/g_{m}=R_{s}$, $R_{F}\to \infty$ is recovered.

With the match constraint (2)

$$R_{F}=R_{in}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}=R_{s}+r_{o}(g_{m}R_{s}-1)\tag{6}$$

So $R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$ are not independent once
$R_{in}=50\Omega$ is imposed. Putting (6) in (4)

$$F\approx 1+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{s}+r_{o}(g_{m}R_{s}-1)}}
+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}} \tag{7}$$

For $A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$

$$R_{F}\approx R_{s}g_{m}r_{o}=R_{s}A_{0}$$

$$F\approx 1+{{1}\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}
=1+{{1}\over {g_{m}}}\left({{1}\over {r_{o}}}+{{\gamma}\over {R_{s}}}\right)\tag{8}$$

I. e. for fixed $R_{in}$

* {\it increasing $R_{F}$ without increasing loop gain
destroys the match.}
* decreasing $F$ needs {\it increasing loop gain $A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}$},
i. e. increasing $R_{F}$ {\it and} $g_{m}r_{o}$
together according to (6).

In (8) $F\to 1$ monotonically for $g_{m}\to \infty$ and
for $r_{o}\to \infty$. In practice:

* Maximise $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ for the power you can
afford.  $g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W I_{D}}$ in strong inversion,
$\propto I_{D}$ in weak inversion, so weak-moderate inversion
is $g_{m}/I_{D}$ optimum.  Increase $W_{1},W_{2}$ and $I_{D}$
until the input pole

$$\omega_{in}\approx {1\over {R_{s}C_{in}}},\qquad
C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+|A_{v}|)C_{gd}$$

falls on the band edge, Miller effect included.
Multi finger layout to keep $R_{g}\ll R_{s}$.

* Maximise $r_{o}$ at that current: longer $L$, cascode the
inverter - $r_{o}\to g_{m,cas}r_{o,cas}r_{o}$ - retro-cascode
self biased LNA. This lets you use a much larger $R_{F}$ for
the same $50\Omega $, cf. (6), and kills the $R_{s}/R_{F}$
term. Short channel $A_{0}\approx 8-15$, cascoded $A_{0}\approx 30-50$.

Then set

$$R_{F}=50(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}$$

for the $g_{m},r_{o}$ you have. E. g. $r_{o}=300\Omega $,
$g_{m}=20\,{\rm mS}$, $A_{0}=6$, $R_{F}\approx 50\Omega $,
$F\approx 1+0.17+0.67\approx 1.84=2.6\,{\rm dB}$ for
$\gamma\approx 1$.  Doubling $g_{m}$ to $40\,{\rm mS}$ with
$r_{o}=250\Omega $, $A_{0}=10$, $R_{F}\approx 300\Omega $,
$F\approx 1+0.17+0.33\approx 1.5=1.8\,{\rm dB}$.

* Optimise the split $g_{m1}$ vs $g_{m2}$,
Eq.5.  For $\gamma_{n}\approx \gamma_{p}$ the split cancels to
first order.  Usually $W_{p}\approx (\mu_{n}/\mu_{p})W_{n}$ for
symmetrical inverter $V_{o,DC}\approx V_{DD}/2$ maximum
swing and $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$.  If $\gamma_{p}<\gamma_{n}$
weight to the p-device.

With unbounded $g_{m}r_{o}$ the only limit is power and
$C_{in}$ bandwidth and $R_{g}$, induced gate noise. Power
constrained optimum is

$${\rm min}\;F\;{\rm s.t.}\;R_{in}=50,\;P_{DC}=V_{DD}I_{D}=const.,
\;C_{in}<1/R_{s}\omega_{0}$$

swept with $g_{m}/I_{D}$ methodology in simulation.

In a narrow band design $R_{F}$ can be made noiseless by
replacing it by $L_{F}$ or transformer feedback. In wide band
the $R_{s}/R_{F}$ vs $R_{in}$ trade off is fundamentally broken
by {\it noise cancelling}: sense the noise voltage at the
matching node with an auxiliary amplifier $A_{aux}=-1-R_{F}/R_{s}$
and add it in phase to the signal so that $i_{n,R_{F}}$ and
$i_{n,D}$ cancel, Bruccoleri et al. JSSC 2005. Then $R_{in}$
can be $50\Omega $ with $F\approx 1+\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$ with no
$R_{s}/R_{F}$ penalty, $<2\,{\rm dB}$ in deep sub micron CMOS.

> {\it In short: keep $R_{in}=50$ by keeping
> $R_{F}=R_{in}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}$. The only way to lower
> $F\approx 1+R_{s}/R_{F}+\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$ without
> changing $R_{in}$ is to raise the open loop gain.
> Raise $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ and $r_{o}$ - larger $W$, larger
> $I_{D}$, longer $L$ or cascodes - and raise $R_{F}$
> proportionally. In the limit $F=1+(1/r_{o}+\gamma/R_{s})/g_{m}$.
> Practically 20-40 mS total $g_{m}$ with $A_{0}>10$ gives
> $R_{F}=200-500\Omega $ and $NF=2-3\,{\rm dB}$ wideband,
> $<2\,{\rm dB}$ with cascoding or noise cancellation. The
> optimum power constrained $W$ is the largest $W$ that still meets
> the $1/R_{s}C_{in}$ bandwidth.}

answer.text:
For a first order it is the :

$${\cal T}_{v}={\cal T}_{i}={\cal R}_{m}
\sim  -R_{F}$$ inverting shunt-shunt amplifier.

$$R_{in}= {V_{t}\over I_{t}}\approx 
{R_{F}+r_{o}\over 1+g_{m}r_{o}}\approx {R_{F}\over 1+g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}}
\approx {1\over g_{m}}\;\;,\;g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;,\;\;
r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{1}$$

in the normal high gain limit $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$ and
$r_{o}\gg R_{F}$ and

$$A_{v0}=-g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}\approx -g_{m}R_{F}\tag{2}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}\over 1-A_{v0}}\tag{3}$$

$A_{v}$ is the open loop voltage gain of the
inverter.

> {\it I.E. $R_{in}$ is $R_{F}$ divided by the amount of
> feed back. For $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty$ $R_{in}\rightarrow
> 1/g_{m}$ independent of $R_{F}$ to first order.}

With (1) the matching condition ``50 Ohm'' {\it fixes}
$g_{m}$ and $R_{F}$ to one relation, for $r_{o}\rightarrow
\infty$ it fixes $g_{m}$ itself:

$$R_{in}=R_{s}=50\;\;\to\;\; g_{m}\approx 1/R_{s}=20{\rm mS}
\tag{4a}$$

$$R_{F}=R_{s}\left( 1+g_{m}r_{o}\right)-r_{o}\approx g_{m}r_{o}R_{s}
\;\;,\;\;r_{o}<\infty \tag{4b}$$

Small signal nodal with $G_{s}=1/R_{s}\;,\;G_{F}=1/R_{F}\;,\;
G_{o}=1/r_{o}$ :

$$\eqalign{
\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)V_{in}-G_{F}V_{out}&=G_{s}V_{s}\cr
\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)V_{in}+\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)V_{out}&=0}$$

$${\cal D}=G_{s}\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)+G_{F}\left(G_{o}+g_{m}\right)$$

$$A_{v}={V_{out}\over V_{s}}=-G_{s}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)/{\cal D}
\tag{5}$$

Put noise current sources in parallel with $R_{F}$ and in
parallel with $r_{o}$

$$\eqalign{
\overline{I_{nF}^{2}}&=4kTG_{F}\cr
\overline{I_{nD}^{2}}&=4kT\gamma g_{m}\cr
&\gamma \approx {2\over 3}-2-3\;{\rm in\;short\;ch.}\cr
\overline{V_{nRs}^{2}}&=4kTR_{s}}$$

$$\eqalign{
\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)V_{in}-G_{F}V_{out}&=-I_{nF}\cr
\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)V_{in}+\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)V_{out}&=
+I_{nF}} \tag{6a}$$

$$\eqalign{
\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)V_{in}-G_{F}V_{out}&=0\cr
\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)V_{in}+\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)V_{out}&=
-I_{nD}} \tag{6b}$$

$$\eqalign{
{|V_{out}|^{2}_{F}&=|I_{nF}|^{2}\left(G_{s}+g_{m}\right)^{2}/{\cal D}^{2}\cr
|V_{out}|^{2}_{D}&=|I_{nD}|^{2}\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)^{2}/{\cal D}^{2}\cr
|V_{out}|^{2}_{Rs}&=|V_{nRs}|^{2}G_{s}^{2}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)^{2}
/{\cal D}^{2}}$$

i. e. with $F$ the conventional $SNR_{in}/SNR_{out}$

$$F=1+{ |V_{out}|^{2}_{F}+|V_{out}|^{2}_{D}\over
|V_{out}|^{2}_{Rs}} \tag{7}$$

$$F=1+{G_{F}\left(G_{s}+g_{m}\right)^{2}\over
G_{s}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)^{2}}+
\gamma g_{m}{\left(G_{s}+G_{F}\right)^{2}\over
G_{s}\left(g_{m}-G_{F}\right)^{2}} \tag{8}$$

For $g_{m}\gg G_{F}$

$$F\approx 1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\left(1+{G_{s}\over g_{m}}\right)^{2}
+\gamma {1\over g_{m}G_{s}^{-1}}\left(1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\right)^{2}
\tag{8a}$$

$$F\approx 1+{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\left(1+{1\over g_{m}R_{s}}\right)^{2}+
{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}\left(1+{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\right)^{2}
\approx 1+{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}+{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\tag{8b}$$

up to factors $2-4$ depending on the exact definition of
matching. In the literature you will find often quoted in the
very high gain limit $g_{m}R_{s}\gg 1$

$$F\approx 1+{4R_{s}\over R_{F}}+{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}\tag{9}$$

and, with the matching constraint enforced, e. g. $G_{o}\to 0$,
$R_{in}=1/g_{m}=R_{s}$:

$$F_{|matched, r_{o}\to \infty}=
1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\left(1+1\right)^{2}+
\gamma \left(1+{G_{F}\over G_{s}}\right)^{2}
\approx 1+\gamma +4{R_{s}\over R_{F}}\tag{10}$$

* the $R_{s}/R_{F}$ term is the $4kTR_{F}$ noise divided
by the loop gain. It is made small by making $R_{F}$ large.

* the $\gamma /g_{m}R_{s}$ term is the channel noise of the
inverter referred to the source. For the usual inverter
$\gamma g_{m}= \gamma_{n}g_{m1}+\gamma_{p}g_{m2}$.
It is made small by making $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ large.

Under the constraint (4) $R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$ are not
independent. Imposing $R_{in}=R_{s}$ :

$${\cal D}_{|match}=2G_{s}\left(G_{o}+G_{F}\right)=
2G_{F}\left(G_{o}+g_{m}\right) \tag{11}$$

$$G_{F}=G_{s}{G_{o}\over G_{o}+g_{m}-G_{s}}=
{R_{s}^{-1}r_{o}^{-1}\over r_{o}^{-1}+g_{m}-R_{s}^{-1}}\tag{12}$$

Put it in (8):

$$F_{|match}=1+{x(1+y)^{2}+\gamma y(1+x)^{2}\over (y-x)^{2}}\tag{13}$$

$$x={G_{F}\over G_{s}}={R_{s}\over R_{F}}\;\;,\;\;
y={g_{m}\over G_{s}}=g_{m}R_{s}\;\;,\;\;z={G_{o}\over G_{s}}=
{R_{s}\over r_{o}}$$

with $z+x=x(z+y)$ from the match. For $z\to 0$,
$y\to 1$. I.E. to first order fixing the match
fixes $g_{m}$. Then (13) $\to 1+\gamma$ for
$x\to 0$, $R_{F}\to \infty$.

For $z\ne 0$ you can let $x\to 0$ and

$$y\approx 1+z/x\gg 1\tag{14}$$

$$F_{|match}\approx 1+ x +{\gamma\over y}\to 1\tag{15}$$

I.E. in principle $F\to 1$, $NF\to 0\,{\rm dB}$ for
$y=g_{m}R_{s}\to \infty$, $R_{F}\to \infty$ with (4b)
satisfied.

Physically: increase the open loop gain $|A_{v0}|=
g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}$ . Then for the same
$R_{in}=R_{F}/(1+|A_{v0}|)=R_{s}$ you can afford a
larger $R_{F}$ - less $R_{F}$ noise - and a larger
$g_{m}$ - less $g_{m}$ noise referred to input.

So the recipe for the topology as drawn - a self
biased shunt-shunt current reuse inverter - is:

* current reuse is already optimum: $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$
for the same $I_{D}$. So for a given power you get
$\times 2$ $g_{m}$. Size $M_{1},M_{2}$ so that
$g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$. I. e. $W_{p}\approx 2-3\,W_{n}$
for equal $g_{m}$.

* make $g_{m}R_{s}$ as large as power allows and make
$R_{F}$ as large as (4b) allows. In practice for
$r_{o}=\infty$, $R_{F}$ is free to first order and
$$NF_{min}\approx 10\log\left[1+{\gamma\over g_{m}R_{s}}\right]
\approx 10\log\,(1+\gamma)\approx 2-3.5\,{\rm dB}
\tag{16}$$
for $g_{m}R_{s}=1$, $\gamma =0.7-1.5$.

With finite $r_{o}$

$$R_{F}=R_{s}+r_{o}\left(g_{m}R_{s}-1\right) \tag{17}$$

so every increase of $g_{m}$ must be accompanied by an
increase of $R_{F}$ to keep $R_{in}=50\,{\rm \Omega}$.

Typical $0.18\mu$, $1.8\,{\rm V}$, $2-5\,{\rm mA}$:
$g_{m}\approx 20-40\,{\rm mS}$, $r_{o}\approx 0.5-2\,{\rm k\Omega}$,
$|A_{v0}|\approx 10-20$, $R_{F}\approx 200-800\,{\rm \Omega}$,
$|A_{v}|\approx R_{F}/R_{s}\approx 4-16$, $NF\approx 2.5-4\,{\rm dB}$.
Doubling $g_{m}$ to $40\,{\rm mS}$ and putting
$R_{F}\approx 500-1k$ brings (8) down by $\approx 1\,{\rm dB}$
at the price of $\approx \times 2$ power and
$\propto W_{g}C_{gs}$ input capacitance.

The limits are:

* power $P=V_{DD}I_{D}$, $g_{m}\propto I_{D}/V_{ov}$,
$g_{m}/I_{D}$ max. $\approx 15-20\,{\rm S/A}$ in
moderate inversion.

* $r_{o}\propto 1/\lambda I_{D}\propto L/I_{D}$, cascode
to boost $r_{o}$ and allow larger $R_{F}$ for the same
$g_{m}$ without extra power.

* bandwidth / stability. Input pole
$\omega_{in}\approx \left(1+g_{m}r_{o}\right)/R_{F}C_{in}$,
$C_{in}=C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd}(1+g_{m}R_{F})+C_{pad}$,
output pole $\omega_{out}\approx 1/r_{o}C_{out}$.
Large $R_{F},g_{m},W_{g}$ quickly make the two pole
system unstable. Add $C_{F}$ compensation or series
peaking $L_{g}$.

* headroom: the self biased inverter $V_{in,DC}=V_{out,DC}$
$\approx V_{DD}/2$ for $ \beta_{n}\approx \beta_{p}$,
set by $R_{F}$. Large $R_{F}$ makes bias very
sensitive.

If $2-3\,{\rm dB}$ is not enough, the shunt $R_{F}$
topology cannot be noise and power matched simultaneously
with a noiseless match. You have to resort to
transformer, inductive degeneration, capacitive
noiseless feedback or, most common today, noise
cancelling: sense the $R_{F}$ and $M_{1,2}$ noise at
the input node with an auxiliary $g_{mA}$ stage and
subtract it at the output. In ideal cancellation the
$R_{s}/R_{F}$ and a large part of $\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$
terms are cancelled, $R_{in}$ remaining $\approx 1/g_{m}$
while $NF\to 1+\gamma_{A}/g_{mA}R_{s}$, $<2\,{\rm dB}$
is routinely achieved.

answer.text:
The self biased inverter with $R_{F}$ is a shunt-shunt
wideband LNA. Let

$$G_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;,\;\;R_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\;\;,\;\;
G_{s}=1/R_{s}$$

$R_{s}=50\,\Omega$, $R_{F}=1/G_{F}$, $R_{o}=1/G_{o}$.
Put $V_{i}$ at the gates, $V_{o}$ at the drains.

$$\begin{aligned}
{\rm at}\;V_{i}:&\;(V_{i}-V_{s})G_{s}+(V_{i}-V_{o})G_{F}=0\\
{\rm at}\;V_{o}:&\;(V_{o}-V_{i})G_{F}+V_{o}G_{o}+G_{m}V_{i}=0
\end{aligned}$$

apart from noise. Hence with $V_{s}=0$

$$\frac{V_{o}}{V_{i}}=\frac{1-G_{m}R_{F}}{1+R_{F}/R_{o}}
\approx -G_{m}(R_{o}\parallel R_{F}) $$

and the current injected in $V_{i}$ is $(V_{i}-V_{o})/R_{F}$ :

$$R_{in}=\frac{R_{F}}{1-V_{o}/V_{i}}=\frac{R_{o}+R_{F}}{1+G_{m}R_{o}} $$

i.e.

$$G_{in}=\frac1{R_{in}}=\frac{G_{F}(G_{o}+G_{m})}{G_{F}+G_{o}} $$

Matching $R_{in}=R_{s}$ :

$$G_{s}=G_{F}\frac{G_{o}+G_{m}}{G_{F}+G_{o}} \tag{1}$$

For $R_{o}\to\infty$ :

$$R_{in}\approx \frac1{G_{m}} $$

so matching requires

$$g_{m1}+g_{m2}\approx 1/R_{s}=20\,{\rm mS}$$

In general

$$G_{m}=\frac1{R_{s}}\left(1+\frac{R_{F}}{R_{o}}\right)-\frac1{R_{o}}
\approx \frac1{R_{s}}\left(1+\frac{R_{F}}{R_{o}}\right) \tag{2}$$

i.e. finite $R_{o}$ needs larger $G_{m}$.

Closed loop gain from source:

$$A_{v}=\frac{V_{o}}{V_{s}}=
-\frac{G_{s}(G_{m}-G_{F})}{\Delta}$$

$$\Delta =G_{s}(G_{F}+G_{o})+G_{F}(G_{o}+G_{m})$$

With (1), $\Delta =2G_{s}(G_{F}+G_{o})$ and for
$G_{m}\gg G_{F}$,

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{R_{F}}{2R_{s}}\frac{1}{1+R_{s}/(R_{o}+R_{F})}$$

Noise. $R_{F}$ : $4kTG_{F}$, M1,M2 :
$4kT\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+4kT\gamma_{2}g_{m2}$ at the output
node. With the same nodal equations,

output due to $R_{F}$ current $i_{nF}$ :

$$\frac{V_{o}}{i_{nF}}=\frac{G_{s}+G_{m}}{\Delta}=Z_{F}$$

output due to MOS current $i_{nM}$ :

$$\frac{V_{o}}{i_{nM}}=-\frac{G_{s}+G_{F}}{\Delta}=Z_{M}$$

Output noise due to $R_{s}$ alone is $|A_{v}|^{2}4kTR_{s}$.
Hence noise factor $F$ :

$$F=1+\frac{|Z_{F}|^{2}4kTG_{F}+|Z_{M}|^{2}4kT(\gamma_{1}g_{m1}
+\gamma_{2}g_{m2})}{|A_{v}|^{2}4kTR_{s}}$$

$$F=1+\frac{(G_{s}+G_{m})^{2}G_{F}+(G_{s}+G_{F})^{2}
(\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+\gamma_{2}g_{m2})}
{G_{s}(G_{m}-G_{F})^{2}} \tag{3}$$

$R_{o}$ enters only via the matching condition (1).
For $R_{o}\to\infty$, $G_{m}=G_{s}$,

$$Z_{F}\approx R_{F},\;Z_{M}\approx -R_{F}/2,\;
A_{v}\approx -R_{F}/2R_{s}$$

$$F\approx 1+\frac{4R_{s}}{R_{F}}+R_{s}(\gamma_{1}g_{m1}
+\gamma_{2}g_{m2}) $$

and with $R_{s}G_{m}=1$,

$$F\approx 1+\frac{4R_{s}}{R_{F}}+\gamma_{eff} \tag{4}$$

$$\gamma_{eff}=\frac{\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+\gamma_{2}g_{m2}}
{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}$$

This is the intuition. The $4R_{s}/R_{F}$ is the
$R_{F}$ contribution, the $\gamma_{eff}$ is the
channel contribution referred with the match.

With finite $R_{o}$, neglecting $G_{F}$ against
$G_{s},G_{m}$ in (3),

$$F\approx 1+\frac{R_{s}}{R_{F}}
\frac{(2+R_{F}/R_{o})^{2}}{(1+R_{F}/R_{o})^{2}}
+\frac{\gamma_{eff}}{1+R_{F}/R_{o}} \tag{5}$$

with (2), $1+R_{F}/R_{o}\approx G_{m}R_{s}$.

Both terms decrease when $R_{F}$ is made large.
In the limit $R_{F}\to\infty$ :

$$F_{min}\to 1+\gamma_{eff}$$

i.e. $\sim 2.2\,$dB long channel $\gamma=2/3$,
$\sim 3-4\,$dB nano-CMOS.

Therefore for fixed $R_{in}=50\,\Omega$:

* keep (1)-(2) satisfied,
* maximize $R_{F}$.

Increasing $R_{F}$ raises $R_{in}$. To bring $R_{in}$
back to $50\,\Omega$ you must increase $G_{m}$ per (2).
In practice:

1. Self bias at $V_{in,DC}=V_{o,DC}\approx V_{DD}/2$
for swing. That fixes $W_{2}/W_{1}\approx
\mu_{n}/\mu_{p}$ to first order, i.e. $g_{m1}\approx
g_{m2}$. This also essentially minimizes
$\gamma_{eff}$ unless $\gamma_{n}$ and $\gamma_{p}$
are very different, and gives current-reuse:
same $I_{D}$ gives $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$.

2. Use short $L$ for $f_{T}$ but not so short that
$R_{o}$ collapses and $\gamma$ explodes. $R_{F}$
is limited by intrinsic gain. From (1):

$$R_{F}=R_{s}(1+G_{m}R_{o})-R_{o}\approx R_{s}(1+A_{0})$$

$A_{0}=G_{m}R_{o}$. Scaling $W_{1},W_{2},I_{D}$
together at fixed $V_{ov}$ keeps $A_{0}$ constant,
$R_{F}$ saturates at $R_{s}(1+A_{0})$. Larger $A_{0}$
needs larger $g_{m}/I_{D}$ and larger $L$.

3. Iterative scale-up: start with a $R_{F}$ of a few
$100\,\Omega$, size $W_{1},W_{2}$ for $R_{in}=50$.
Increase $R_{F}$; $R_{in}$ goes high; increase
$W_{1},W_{2}$ proportionally, i.e. increase $I_{D}$
and $G_{m}$, to restore $R_{in}=50$. Gain
$\approx R_{F}/2R_{s}$ goes up, $F$ in (5) goes down.

Price paid:

* power: $G_{m}\approx (1+R_{F}/R_{o})/R_{s}$ must grow.
* bandwidth: input capacitance
$$C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1-A_{v0})(C_{gd1}+C_{gd2})$$
with $A_{v0}=V_{o}/V_{i}\approx -R_{F}/R_{s}$.
 Miller multiplication grows with $R_{F}$, pole at
 $\approx 1/2\pi (R_{s}/2)C_{in}$ moves down.
 Larger $W$ adds $C_{gs},C_{gd}$. This is the
 ultimate NF-BW-power trade-off.
* stability, linearity: larger loop gain and larger
 closed-loop gain give peaking with capacitive load
 and earlier compression, lower IIP3.

In short: under $R_{in}=50\,\Omega$ constraint, lower
NF is obtained by larger $R_{F}$ and correspondingly
larger $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$, i.e. larger devices and current,
up to the point allowed by power, Miller bandwidth,
gain and linearity.

answer.text:
This is a self biased CMOS inverter with shunt-shunt
feedback. Put

$$g_m = g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;,\;\; g_{ds}=g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\;\;,\;\;
r_o =1/g_{ds}$$

DC: no gate current, no DC drop on $R_F$,

$$V_{in,DC}=V_{out,DC}=V_{trip}$$

where $I_{Dn}=I_{Dp}$. $V_{trip}$ is set by the
$P/N$ ratio, $R_F$ is free for AC.

AC small signal, no external load. At the output:

$$\frac{V_y-V_x}{R_F}+g_m V_x+g_{ds}V_y =0$$

At the input with a test current $I_x$ :

$$I_x = \frac{V_x-V_y}{R_F}$$

i.e.

$$\frac{V_y}{V_x} = \frac{1-g_mR_F}{1+g_{ds}R_F}$$

$$R_{in}=\frac{V_x}{I_x}= \frac{1+R_F g_{ds}}{g_m+g_{ds}}
      =\frac{R_F+r_o}{1+g_mr_o} \tag{1}$$

With source $R_s$,

$$\frac{V_x-V_s}{R_s}+\frac{V_x-V_y}{R_F}=0$$

$$\frac{V_y}{V_s}=A_v=\frac{1-g_mR_F}
{1+g_mR_s+g_{ds}R_s+g_{ds}R_F} \tag{2}$$

For $g_mR_F\gg 1$, $r_o$ large,

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{1}{g_m}\;\;,\;\;
A_v \approx -\frac{g_mR_F}{1+g_mR_s}$$

Matched $R_{in}=R_s$:

$$g_m\approx 1/R_s \;\;,\;\; A_v\approx -R_F/2R_s \tag{3}$$

This is only first order. Exactly from (1) $R_{in}=R_s$,

$$1+R_Fg_{ds}=R_s(g_m+g_{ds})$$

$$R_F = R_s +(g_mR_s-1)r_o \tag{4}$$

To have $R_F\gg R_s$ while matched you need
$g_mR_s>1$ and large $r_o$. $R_F\approx g_mr_o R_s$
is essentially the open loop gain times $R_s$.

Noise at low frequency: $R_s$, $R_F$ and the
channel noise of $M_{1,2}$.

Put a current $I_n$ in parallel with $R_F$,
$V_s=0$. Solving the nodal equations,

$$\frac{V_y}{I_n}=Z_{RF}= -\frac{R_F(1+g_mR_s)}
{1+g_mR_s+g_{ds}R_s+g_{ds}R_F} \tag{5}$$

Channel noise can be lumped as a current from
output to ground with

$$\overline{I_{no}^2}=4kT(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})$$

per Hz. With $V_s=0$, injected at output,

$$\frac{V_y}{I_{no}}=Z_{tr}= -\frac{R_s+R_F}
{1+g_mR_s+g_{ds}R_s+g_{ds}R_F} \tag{6}$$

Output noise:

$$S_{out}=|A_v|^2 4kTR_s+|Z_{RF}|^2\frac{4kT}{R_F}
+|Z_{tr}|^2 4kT(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})$$

Noise factor $F=S_{out}/|A_v|^2 4kTR_s$.
Since the denominator $1+g_mR_s+\cdots$ cancels
in the ratios from (2)(5)(6),

$$F=1+\frac{R_F(1+g_mR_s)^2}{R_s(g_mR_F-1)^2}
+\frac{(R_s+R_F)^2}{R_s(g_mR_F-1)^2}
(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2}) \tag{7}$$

For $g_mR_F\gg 1$,

$$F\approx 1+\frac{(1+g_mR_s)^2}{g_m^2R_FR_s}
+\frac{(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})(R_s+R_F)^2}
{R_s\,g_m^2R_F^2} \tag{8}$$

The second term is $R_F$, the third is the FETs.
With match $g_mR_s\approx 1$, $R_F\gg R_s$,

$$F\approx 1+\frac{4R_s}{R_F}
+\frac{\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2}}{g_m}
\frac{1}{g_mR_s} \tag{9}$$

i.e. with $\gamma_{eff}= (\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})/g_m$,

$$F\approx 1+\gamma_{eff}+4R_s/R_F$$

The limiting $F_{min}=1+\gamma_{eff}$, $\approx 3\,$dB
for short channel, can only be approached with
$R_F\gg R_s$.

Hence:

* transistor noise $\propto 1/g_m$, $R_F$ noise
$\propto 1/R_F$. Both want large $g_m$ and large $R_F$.
* they cannot be increased independently because
of (1)(4). Increasing $R_F$ alone raises $R_{in}$
and mismatches. To keep $R_{in}=R_s=50\,\Omega$
you must increase loop gain $g_mr_o$ in proportion:

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_F}{1+|A_{ol}|}$$

So optimization is: increase open-loop gain and
increase $R_F$ together to hold $R_{in}$.

In practice:

1. Size $P/N$ for $V_{trip}\approx V_{DD}/2$ for
headroom. This makes $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$,
maximizing $g_m=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ for the re-used
current. Current re-use is the advantage of the
inverter: $g_m/I_D$ is doubled.

2. Choose $L$ larger than minimum. Larger $L$
gives larger $r_o=1/(\lambda_n+\lambda_p)I_D$,
larger intrinsic gain $g_mr_o$, smaller $\gamma$
and smaller short-channel excess noise, allowing
larger $R_F$ from (4) for the same $g_m$. Too
large $L$ kills $f_T$.

3. For a given $I_D$, maximize $W$, i.e. minimize
$V_{ov}$, maximize $g_m/I_D$, maximize $g_mr_o$.
Then re-choose $R_F$ from (4) to re-match to
$50\,\Omega$. $F$ drops monotonically.

4. Increase $I_D$, i.e. power, with $W$ to keep
$V_{ov}$ moderate. $g_m$ grows, $F_{FET}$ drops.
$R_F$ for match stays roughly $ \sim 2R_s/\lambda V_{ov}$,
set by intrinsic gain.

The scaling is stopped by bandwidth and power.
Larger $W$ means larger $C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}
+$ Miller $C_{gd}$, larger $C_{out}$, lower input
and output poles, degraded $S_{11}$ at high
frequency and lower $f_{-3dB}$. The closed loop
gain $|A_v|\approx R_F/2R_s$ also grows, increasing
Miller effect.

So the constrained optimum is: the largest
inverter $g_mr_o$ and largest $R_F$ that still
satisfy $R_{in}=50\,\Omega$, power budget, and
required $S_{11}$ bandwidth. There is no interior
NF minimum vs $R_F$; NF improves until capacitance
forces you to stop.

answer.text:
This is a self biased CMOS inverter with shunt-shunt
$R_{F}$.

$M_{1},M_{2}$ carry the same DC current $I_{D}$.
$R_{F}$ carries no DC, so

$$V_{G1}=V_{G2}=V_{D1}=V_{D2}=V_{M}$$

both in saturation. AC, with $C_{1}$ short,

$$g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\quad r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

Ignoring load capacitance, KCL at in and out gives

$$R_{in}=\frac{V_{t}}{I_{t}}=\frac{r_{o}+R_{F}}{1+g_{m}r_{o}} \tag{1}$$

Let the source be $R_{s}=50\,\Omega$. Power match is

$$R_{in}=R_{s}$$

i.e.

$$R_{F}=R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}
 =R_{s}+r_{o}(g_{m}R_{s}-1) \tag{2}$$

Raising $g_{m}$ alone lowers $R_{in}$. Raising $R_{F}$
alone raises $R_{in}$. To keep $R_{in}=50$ they
must be raised together.

Closed loop $V_{s}$ to output gain is

$$A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}R_{F}-1}{1+g_{m}R_{s}+ (R_{F}+R_{s})/r_{o}}
\approx -\frac{R_{F}}{2R_{s}} $$

matched, $g_{m}R_{F}\gg 1$. I.e. a transimpedance
$\approx -R_{F}$ driven by $V_{s}/2R_{s}$.

Noise: $4kT/R_{F}$ in parallel with $R_{F}$,
$4kT\gamma_{1}g_{m1}$, $4kT\gamma_{2}g_{m2}$
from drains to ac ground. $r_{o}$ taken noiseless.

Solving the nodal equations with $R_{s}$ at the
input, for MOS current $i_{o}$ injected at the output:

$$\frac{V_{out}}{i_{o}} = \frac{1}{D} , \quad
D=\frac{1+g_{m}R_{s}}{R_{s}+R_{F}}+\frac1{r_{o}} $$

for $R_{F}$ current $i_{RF}$ between output and input:

$$\frac{V_{out}}{i_{RF}} =\frac{g_{m}+1/R_{s}}{\Delta}$$

with $\Delta = (g_{m}+1/R_{s})/R_{F}+G_{1}/r_{o}$,
$G_{1}=1/R_{s}+1/R_{F}$.

$r_{o}$ cancels in the ratio to $A_{v}$:

$$\left|\frac{V_{out,MOS}}{A_{v}}\right| =
 \frac{R_{s}+R_{F}}{g_{m}R_{F}-1}$$

$$\left|\frac{V_{out,RF}}{A_{v}}\right| =
 \frac{(1+g_{m}R_{s})R_{F}}{g_{m}R_{F}-1}$$

Hence with source noise $4kTR_{s}$,

$$\begin{aligned}
F &=1+\frac{\overline{V_{RF}^{2}}+\overline{V_{MOS}^{2}}}
{A_{v}^{2}4kTR_{s}} \\
&=1+\frac{1}{(g_{m}R_{F}-1)^{2}}
\left[\frac{R_{F}}{R_{s}}(1+g_{m}R_{s})^{2}
+\frac{\gamma_{n}g_{mn}+\gamma_{p}g_{mp}}{R_{s}}
(R_{s}+R_{F})^{2}\right]
\end{aligned} \tag{3}$$

For $R_{F}\gg R_{s}$, $g_{m}R_{F}\gg 1$:

$$F\approx 1+
\frac{(1+g_{m}R_{s})^{2}}{g_{m}^{2}R_{F}R_{s}}
+\frac{\gamma_{n}g_{mn}+\gamma_{p}g_{mp}}{g_{m}^{2}R_{s}} \tag{4}$$

$$F_{RF}+F_{MOS}$$

If $g_{m}R_{s}=1$, i.e. $R_{in}\approx 1/g_{m}$ for
$r_{o}\to\infty$:

$$F\approx 1+\gamma_{eff}+4\frac{R_{s}}{R_{F}}$$

If $g_{m}R_{s}>1$, large loop gain:

$$F\approx 1+\frac{\gamma_{eff}}{g_{m}R_{s}}+\frac{R_{s}}{R_{F}} \tag{5}$$
$$\gamma_{eff}= \frac{\gamma_{n}g_{mn}+\gamma_{p}g_{mp}}
{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}$$

Both terms fall with larger $g_{m}$ and larger $R_{F}$.
Unlike a common-gate where $g_{m}=1/R_{s}$ is frozen
by match to $F\ge 1+\gamma$, here (1) gives an
extra degree of freedom. Keep (2) satisfied while
making $g_{m}$ and $R_{F}$ large.

In practice:

* $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ for the same $I_{D}$.
Current reuse. This is the benefit of the inverter.
* Increase $W_{1},W_{2}$, $I_{D}$, i.e. $g_{m}$.
Keep $W_{p}/W_{n}\approx \mu_{n}/\mu_{p}$ so
$V_{M}\approx V_{DD}/2$ for swing and saturation.
$R_{F}$ does not affect DC.
* For each $g_{m},r_{o}$ choose $R_{F}$ from (2)
to get $R_{in}=50$. Approx $R_{F}\approx
R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o})$.
Large $g_{m}r_{o}$ = intrinsic gain allows large
$R_{F}$, i.e. small $R_{s}/R_{F}$ and large gain
$-R_{F}/2R_{s}$, which also suppresses stage 2 by Friis.
* For fixed power, maximize $g_{m}/I_{D}$: large $W$,
small $V_{ov}$, moderate/weak inversion. This raises
$g_{m}$, raises required $R_{F}$, lowers (5).
* $L$: minimum $L$ gives max $f_{T}$, min $C$,
max $g_{m}$ per current, but small $r_{o}$,
small $A_{v0}=g_{m}r_{o}$, small $R_{F}$, larger
$F_{RF}$. Slightly longer $L$ raises $A_{v0}$ and
lowers $\gamma$ at expense of $C$ and $f_{T}$.
Usually $L_{min}$ to $2$-$3\times L_{min}$ is co-optimized.

Limit: power $V_{DD}I_{D}$, $C_{in}\approx
C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+|A_{v}|)(C_{gd1}+C_{gd2})$.
Larger $W$ and larger $|A_{v}|\approx R_{F}/2R_{s}$
Miller-multiply $C_{gd}$, creating the input pole
$1/R_{s}C_{in}$, degrading wideband $S_{11}$ and BW,
output pole, stability and linearity. IIP3 $\propto V_{ov}$
degrades when $W$ is enlarged.

So: size up the inverter for maximum affordable
$g_{m}$, track $R_{F}$ up to hold $R_{in}=50$,
until NF improvement $\propto 1/g_{m}$ is not
worth power, area and BW loss. Ideally $F\to 1$.
Practically 1-3 dB with $g_{m}R_{s}\sim 2$-$5$.

answer.text:
The transistors can be combined into one equivalent device

$$
G_m=g_{m1}+g_{m2},\qquad 
r_o=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2},\qquad 
\bar\gamma=\frac{\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\; .
$$

$M_1$ and $M_2$ carry the same bias current, i.e. the
inverter re-uses the current.

### Input resistance

Neglecting $C_{gs},C_{gd}$ for the moment, nodal analysis gives

$$
A_v\equiv\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}=
\frac{(1-G_mR_F)r_o}{R_F+r_o},
\qquad 
R_{in}= \frac{R_F+r_o}{1+G_m r_o}\; .
$$

For $G_m r_o\gg 1$

$$
R_{in}\;\approx\;\frac1{G_m}\Bigl(1+\frac{R_F}{r_o}\Bigr) .
$$

Imposing the power match $R_{in}=R_S=50\;\Omega$,

$$
\,R_F = R_S\bigl(1+G_m r_o\bigr)-r_o
      \;\approx\;R_S\,G_m r_o\;\qquad (G_mr_o\gg1;\; r_o\gg R_S)
$$

i.e. $R_F$ and $G_m r_o$ cannot be chosen independently.
Increasing $R_F$ alone raises $R_{in}$ above $50\;\Omega$;
increasing $G_m$ alone lowers $R_{in}$ below $50\;\Omega$.
The matched voltage gain is then

$$
\frac{V_{out}}{V_s}\approx
-\,\frac12\Bigl(G_m r_o-\frac{r_o}{R_S}\Bigr)
\approx -\frac{G_m r_o}{2}\approx -\frac{R_F}{2R_S}\; .
$$

### Noise factor

With thermal noise of $R_F$ and channel noise
$4kT(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})$ of $M_{1,2}$,
referred to a source $R_S$,

$$
F = 1+
\frac{\displaystyle
\frac{(G_m+1/R_S)^2}{R_F}
+\bar\gamma G_m\,(1/R_S+1/R_F)^2}
{\displaystyle (G_m-1/R_F)^2/R_S}\; .
$$

For the usual design regime $R_F\gg R_S$, $G_mR_F\gg1$,

$$
\,F\;\approx\;
1+\underbrace{\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{G_mR_S}\Bigr)^{2}\frac{R_S}{R_F}}_{\text{noise of }R_F}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\frac{\bar\gamma}{G_mR_S}}_{\text{noise of }M_{1,2}}\,  .
$$

Now eliminate $R_F$ with the match condition,
$R_S/R_F\approx 1/\big[\,1+G_mr_o-r_o/R_S\,\big]$:

$$
F\;\approx\;1+
\frac{\bigl(1+1/G_mR_S\bigr)^2}
     {\,1+G_mr_o-r_o/R_S\,}
+\frac{\bar\gamma}{G_mR_S}\; .
$$

Both excess terms decrease monotonically when

* $G_mR_S$ is made large — the transistor term $\bar\gamma/G_mR_S$ falls,
  and the factor $(1+1/G_mR_S)^2\to1$;
* $G_m r_o$ is made large — because the match then *allows* a large
  $R_F\approx R_S G_m r_o$, whose noise $R_S/R_F\approx 1/G_mr_o$ falls.

In the ideal thermal-noise model there is therefore no interior
optimum: $F\to 1+1/G_mr_o$ as $G_mR_S\to\infty$. The optimum is on the
boundary set by power, bandwidth and device capacitance.

### Practical optimisation

1. **Move along the $R_{in}=50\;\Omega$ curve:** increase $R_F$ and
   $G_m$ (and $r_o$) together, always $R_F\approx R_S(1+G_mr_o)-r_o$.
   A small $R_F$ chosen to obtain the match with a small $G_m$ is the
   worst choice: $R_F$ noise dominates and the gain is low.

2. **Maximise $G_m$ per unit current.** Use the current reuse:
   size $M_1,M_2$ so the self-bias point (set by $R_F$) is
   $V_M\approx V_{DD}/2$, both devices saturated, $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$
   [$(W/L)_p/(W/L)_n\approx \mu_n/\mu_p$ for equal $L$].
   Bias at low $V_{ov}$ (moderate inversion) for high $g_m/I_D$.

3. **Maximise the intrinsic gain $G_m r_o$.** This sets the noise
   floor $1+1/G_mr_o$ and the largest usable $R_F$. Use $L$ somewhat
   above $L_{\min }$ (higher $r_o$, $\bar\gamma$ closer to $2/3$) as
   long as $f_T\gg f_0$; a cascode would help but is not in the circuit.

4. **Take the largest $R_F$ the specifications allow.**
   $R_F$ sets the matched gain $\approx R_F/2R_S$. The limit is
   closed-loop bandwidth — output pole $\approx
   [2\pi(r_o\parallel(R_F+R_S))C_L]^{-1}$, input Miller pole —
   output swing/linearity and settling, not noise.

5. **Scale $W$ and $I_D$ (power) up last.** Larger $G_m$ costs current
   and $C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+|A_v|)C_{gd}$.
   Stop when $\omega_0R_SC_{in}$ and the induced gate noise
   ($\propto (f_0/f_T)^2$) begin to raise $F$ at $f_0$, or the power
   budget is reached. $C_1$ is just a blocking cap: $1/\omega_0C_1\ll R_S$.

In short: do not match with $R_F$ alone or with $1/G_m$ alone.
Raise the loop gain $G_m r_o$, which lets you raise $R_F$ while
keeping $R_{in}=(R_F+r_o)/(1+G_mr_o)=50\;\Omega$; then $R_F$ noise
$\propto R_S/R_F$ and transistor noise $\propto \bar\gamma/G_mR_S$
both fall, until power, $C_{in}/f_T$ and bandwidth stop the scaling.

answer.text:
The $M_{1}-M_{2}$ pair is a current re-use common source
stage with shunt-shunt feedback.  Put

$$g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\qquad 
r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\qquad A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}$$

$R_{F}$ also self biases the inverter.  To first order,
$r_{o}$ finite,

$$\frac{v_{o}}{v_{i}}\approx -g_{m}\,(r_{o}\!\parallel\! R_{F}) $$

$$ R_{in}= \frac{R_{F}+r_{o}}{1+g_{m}r_{o}}
      \approx \frac1{g_{m}}+\frac{R_{F}}{g_{m}r_{o}}\tag{1} $$
i.e. in the limit $r_{o}\!\gg\! R_{F}$, $R_{in}\approx1/g_{m}$.
$R_{in}=R_{S}=50\;\Omega$ does not fix $R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$
separately, it fixes the combination in (1),

$$\,R_{F}=R_{S}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}\,\tag{2}$$

The noise sources are $4kT/R_{F}$ for $R_{F}$ and
$4kT\gamma_{1,2}g_{m1,2}$ for $M_{1,2}$.  Referred to the
source, with $g_{m}R_{F}\gg1$, $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$,

$$ 
\begin{aligned}
F&\approx 
1+
\underbrace{\frac{R_{S}}{R_{F}}
\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{g_{m}R_{S}}\Bigr)^{2}}_{R_{F}}+
\underbrace{\;
\bar\gamma\,\frac{1}{g_{m}R_{S}}
\Bigl(1+\frac{R_{S}}{R_{F}}\Bigr)^{2}}_{M_{1},M_{2}}  \\
\bar\gamma&=\frac{\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+\gamma_{2}g_{m2}}
                 {g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
\end{aligned}\tag{3}
$$

For $R_{F}\!\gg\! R_{S}$ and $g_{m}R_{S}\gtrsim1$ this is

$$F\;\approx\;1+\frac{R_{S}}{R_{F}}+\frac{\bar\gamma}{g_{m}R_{S}}\;  $$

Both excess terms decrease with $R_{F}$ and with $g_{m}$.
Hence, with (2) imposed, $F$ is decreased monotonically
by increasing the loop gain $g_{m}r_{o}$, i.e. by increasing
$R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$ together so that (1) stays $50\;\Omega$.
In the usual textbook limit $R_{in}\approx1/g_{m}$,
$g_{m}=1/R_{S}=20\,{\rm mS}$ is pinned and (3) tends to
$F\to1+\bar\gamma$ for $R_{F}\to\infty$.

In practice:

* Use the current reuse fully. For a given $I_{D}$ both
devices give transconductance. Size for
$g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$, i.e. $(W/L)_{2}/(W/L)_{1}\approx
\mu_{n}/\mu_{p}$, $V_{ov1}\approx V_{ov2}$, output bias
$\approx V_{DD}/2$. Then $\bar\gamma\approx(\gamma_{1}+
\gamma_{2})/2$, at minimum $I_{D}$ - i.e. at the largest
$g_{m}/I_{D}$ compatible with $f_{T}\gg f_{0}$.  Allocating
more $g_{m}$ to the lower-$\gamma$ device lowers
$\bar\gamma$ in (3).

* Make $r_{o}$, hence $A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}$, as large as the
bandwidth allows, e.g. $L$ a few times $L_{\min }$.
A large $A_{0}$ is what allows a large $R_{F}$ in (2)
while keeping $R_{in}=50\;\Omega$.

* Choose $R_{F}$ from the match, eq. (2), not independently.
Increasing the intended $R_{F}$ must be accompanied by the
increase in $g_{m}r_{o}$ in (2).  A useful target is
$R_{F}=(5\!-\!10)R_{S}$ and $g_{m}R_{S}=2\!-\!5$, so that
$R_{S}/R_{F}\ll\bar\gamma/g_{m}R_{S}\ll1$ in (3).

The increase in $R_{F}$ - and in $g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{F})$ -
is stopped in a real design by the required gain,
the output pole $(r_{o}\parallel R_{F})C_{L}$, the input
Miller capacitance, power, and by loss of feedback, i.e.
linearity.  Up to those limits, larger $R_{F}$ with
proportionally larger loop gain, at fixed $R_{in}=50\;\Omega$,
is the NF optimum.

answer.text:
The circuit is a self-biased inverter with shunt-shunt feedback. $C_1$
is an ac short. Put

$$
G_m=g_{m1}+g_{m2},\qquad 
r_o=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2},\qquad 
\bar i_{nd}^{2}=4kT(\gamma_n g_{m1}+\gamma_p g_{m2})\Delta f
      =4kT\gamma_{\rm eff}G_m\Delta f
$$
$$
\gamma_{\rm eff}=\frac{\gamma_n g_{m1}+\gamma_p g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}} .
$$

Both devices carry the same $I_D$; the inverter is a current-reuse
stage, $G_m$ being obtained for roughly half the current of a
single device.

### Input resistance and gain

Applying a test voltage at the gate node,

$$
\,R_{in}=\frac{R_F+r_o}{1+G_m r_o}\approx \frac1{G_m}+\frac{R_F}{G_mr_o}\,\qquad (1)
$$

$$
A_v\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_g}=-
\bigl(G_m-1/R_F\bigr)(r_o\parallel R_F)\approx -G_mr_o
\qquad G_mR_F\gg1,\;R_F\gg r_o
$$

At match $v_g=v_s/2$, so the source-to-output gain is $\approx A_v/2$.
From (1), $R_{in}=R_S=50\;\Omega$ fixes $R_F$ once $G_m$ and $r_o$
are chosen:

$$
\,R_F=R_S(1+G_mr_o)-r_o\, \qquad (2)
$$

$R_F$ alone does not fix $R_{in}$.

### Noise factor

The uncorrelated sources are $R_S$, $R_F$ and the two channel-noise
currents. Referring their output noise to the noise of $R_S$ at the
output gives, exactly to first order in $r_o$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
F=1&+\frac{R_F}{R_S}\,
      \frac{(1+G_mR_S)^2}{(G_mR_F-1)^2}
     +\frac{\gamma_{\rm eff}G_m}{R_S}
      \left[\frac{R_S+R_F}{G_mR_F-1}\right]^2 \\[2mm]
\approx 1&+
\underbrace{\frac{R_S}{R_F}\Bigl(1+\frac1{G_mR_S}\Bigr)^2}_{\text{feedback resistor}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\frac{\gamma_{\rm eff}}{G_mR_S}
      \Bigl(1+\frac{R_S}{R_F}\Bigr)^2}_{\text{$M_1,M_2$}}
\qquad G_mR_F\gg1 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

In the useful regime $G_mR_S\gg1$, $R_F\gg R_S$,

$$
\,F\;\approx\;1+\frac{R_S}{R_F}+\frac{\gamma_{\rm eff}}{G_mR_S}\,\qquad 
NF=10\log_{10}F \tag{4}
$$

### What the $50\;\Omega$ constraint does

Equation (4) says $F$ falls if $R_F$ is increased and if $G_m$ is
increased.  But (1)-(2) forbid increasing either one alone: raising
$R_F$ alone raises $R_{in}$ above $50\;\Omega$; raising $G_m$ alone
lowers $R_{in}$ below $50\;\Omega$.  They must be raised together,
keeping (2) satisfied.  Indeed, for $G_mR_S\gg1$, (2) gives
$R_F/R_S\approx G_mr_o$, so (4) becomes approximately

$$
F-1\;\approx\;\frac{1}{G_mr_o}+\frac{\gamma_{\rm eff}}{G_mR_S}\; .
\tag{5}
$$

In the ideal $g_m,r_o$ model there is no interior minimum: $NF$
decreases monotonically with the loop gain.  The design problem is
therefore to maximise $G_mR_S$ and the intrinsic gain $G_mr_o$
subject to the power, bandwidth, headroom and linearity budget,
and then set $R_F$ from (2).  In practice:

1. **Maximise $G_m$ per unit current.** Keep $V_{ov1},V_{ov2}$ low,
   typically $150$--$200\,{\rm mV}$, and scale $W$ and $I_D$ together
   so $V_{ov}$ and $G_mr_o$ stay high while $G_m$ grows. Size $M_2$
   wider than $M_1$ by $\approx\mu_n/\mu_p$ so $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$,
   the trip point is near $V_{DD}/2$, and $\gamma_{\rm eff}\approx
   (\gamma_n+\gamma_p)/2$.  A device made to carry most of $G_m$ with
   the smaller $\gamma$ helps only marginally and usually destroys
   $r_o$ and symmetry.

2. **Maximise $r_o$ for that $G_m$.** Long enough channels / low
   $V_{ov}$ raise $G_mr_o$, which by (2) permits a large $R_F$ and
   makes the $R_F$ term in (5), $\approx1/G_mr_o$, small. Channel
   length is stopped by the output pole $1/r_oC_L$ and by $f_T$.

3. **Set $R_F$ from the match, Eq. (2),** not from the gain: with
   $R_F\gg r_o$ the gain has already saturated at $\approx-G_mr_o$.

4. **Stop scaling when a practical limit is hit.** Scaling $W,I_D$
   at fixed $V_{ov}$ raises $C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+|A_v|)(C_{gd1}+C_{gd2})$
   in proportion to $G_m$; the input pole $\approx
   [(R_S\parallel R_{in})C_{in}]^{-1}$, the output pole, power and
   output swing/IIP3 then set the largest usable $G_m$.  Beyond the
   point where, from (4), $\gamma_{\rm eff}/G_mR_S\approx R_S/R_F$,
   one source dominates and further improvement is very slow.

Example of the trend: $G_mR_S=5$, $G_mr_o=20$ gives $R_F\approx850\;\Omega$
from (2) and $F\approx1+0.06+0.19$, i.e. of order $1\,{\rm dB}$ before
capacitive, induced-gate and loss effects are included.

In short: do not optimise $R_F$ in isolation. Increase $G_m$ (and
$G_mr_o$) as far as power/bandwidth allow, increase $R_F$
concomitantly to keep $R_{in}=(R_F+r_o)/(1+G_mr_o)=50\;\Omega$, with
$g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$.  The attainable floor is set by Eq. (5).

answer.text:
To optimize the circuit for noise figure (NF) while maintaining Rin at 50 Ohm, we need to consider the noise contributions from each component and their impact on the overall NF. Here's a step-by-step approach:

1. **Identify Noise Sources**: The main noise sources in the circuit are the resistors (Rin, RF, M1, M2) and the capacitor (C1). Each resistor contributes thermal noise, and the capacitor can introduce noise due to its dielectric properties.

2. **Calculate Noise Contributions**:
   - **Thermal Noise**: For resistors, the noise voltage is given by \( V_n = \sqrt{4kTR\Delta f} \), where \( k \) is Boltzmann's constant, \( T \) is the temperature, \( R \) is the resistance, and \( \Delta f \) is the bandwidth.
   - **Capacitor Noise**: The noise from the capacitor is typically negligible compared to resistor noise in most practical scenarios.

3. **Optimize Resistor Values**:
   - **Rin**: Since Rin must remain 50 Ohm, we cannot change its value.
   - **RF**: The feedback resistor RF can be adjusted to minimize the overall NF. A lower RF will reduce the gain of the circuit, which can help in reducing the noise contribution from the feedback network.

For the resistively-shunted common-source LNA the small–signal input resistance and the noise factor can be written very compactly:

1. Input resistance  
   Rin = Rf /( 1 + gm Rf )

2. Noise factor (long-channel MOS, ro  ≫ Rf , neglect gmb)  
   F ≃ 1 + γ /(gm Rs) + Rf /Rs · 1 /(1 + gm Rf )²         (Rs = 50 Ω)

Because the gate is open-circuited, the only independent design variables that remain are gm (set by the bias current and the device width of M1) and the feedback resistor Rf ; M2 can be regarded as an ideal, noiseless current source if it is cascoded properly.

50-Ω broadband matching fixes one relation between gm and Rf:

Rin = 50 Ω  ⇒  50 = Rf /(1 + gm Rf )  ⇒  gm = 1/50 – 1/Rf

or, more conveniently,

gm Rf = A          with        A = Rf /50 – 1                 (1)

so that Rf = 50 (1 + A) and gm = A /[ 50 (1 + A) ].

Insert (1) in the noise expression:

F = 1 + γ + γ/A + 1 /(1 + A)                               (2)

dF/dA = – γ /A² – 1 /(1 + A)²   < 0     for every   A > 0

Equation (2) shows that the excess noise figure is a monotonically decreasing
function of A = gm Rf .  In other words:

• The larger the transconductance gm (hence the larger the dc current you can afford) the lower the noise figure.  
• Rf must be increased at the same time according to (1) so that the real input impedance stays at 50 Ω.  
• As A → ∞ the two additional terms in (2) vanish and the minimum attainable noise factor approaches

        Fmin ≃ 1 + γ      ( ≈ 1.6…1.8   ⇒   NFmin ≈ 2…2.5 dB in CMOS )

Therefore, when 50-Ω matching has to be maintained, there is only one way to optimise the NF:

1. Spend as much bias current as the power budget allows and size M1 as wide as necessary to obtain the largest possible gm.  
2. Choose the feedback resistor from Rf = 50 (1 + gm·50) to keep Rin = 50 Ω.  
3. Make M2 a low-noise cascode (large gds, small γ) so that it adds negligible extra noise.

Once the maximum gm that the power budget allows has been selected, the noise figure is fixed; no further adjustment of Rf, of the over-drive voltage, or of any other linear parameter can lower the NF without breaking the 50-Ω match.

          gm,opt = 1 / 50 Ω  ≃ 20 mS

          Id  =  gm · (VGS – VTH)/α        (α ≃ 1 in strong inversion)

2. Make the feedback resistor as large as practicable.

   (id,n² = 4kT γ gm) and the Johnson noise of RF
   (iRF,n² = 4kT / RF).  Re-refering them to the 50-Ω input gives

          (en,MOS)² = (4kT γ gm) / gm² = 4kT γ RS
          (en,RF )² = (4kT / RF) RS²   = 4kT RS / RF · RS

   The overall noise factor becomes

          F  = 1 + γ            (MOS contribution)
                 + RS / RF       (feedback resistor)

   where γ ≃ 2/3 (long channel) … 1 (deep-sub-µ).

   • NF therefore approaches the theoretical minimum  

          Fmin = 1 + γ   (≈ 1.6…2.0, i.e. 1.8–3 dB)

     as soon as RF ≫ RS.  In practice a few kilo-ohms (1–5 kΩ) already
     makes RS/RF < 0.05, i.e. < 0.2 dB extra noise.

   • Increasing RF further no longer changes Rin, so the only real
     limitation is head-room for bias feedback, resistor area, and
     stability at very low frequencies.

3. Keep the remaining noise terms small.

   • Layout M1 with many short fingers to lower the distributed gate
     resistance RG; its thermal noise appears in series with the signal
     but does not affect the 50 Ω match.

   • Make the cascode device M2 just large enough for gain and voltage
     head-room; its channel noise is divided by the large ro2 and adds
     only a small fraction to F.

   • Choose the “quietest” transistor option the process offers
     (longer channel, thick-oxide if fT margin allows) to minimise γ.

4. There is no benefit in biasing harder than needed for gm = 20 mS;
   gm is fixed by the matching requirement, so extra current only wastes
   power without lowering NF.

Summary of the optimisation steps when Rin must stay at 50 Ω:

2. Use the largest RF that still lets the DC feedback bias work
   (kΩ-range).

The input is applied to the gate of M1 and the 50 Ω antenna (or test generator) is coupled through C1.  
The only way the antenna “sees” exactly 50 Ω is through the shunt-feedback loop formed by R​F and the intrinsic transconductance of M1.  
With the small-signal model of the cell one obtains    

          Rin = (1 + gds R​F)/(gm + gds)  ≈ 1/gm                ( ro (=1/gds) » 50 Ω )

Hence, as long as we keep ro of M1 reasonably large, the input match is fixed almost exclusively by gm:

          gm ≃ 1/Rin = 1/50 Ω ≃ 20 mS                       (1)

If we try to increase gm any further the input resistance would fall below 50 Ω, so we would have to raise R​F in exactly the amount required by (1) to keep the product in (1) unchanged.  
In other words, the 50 Ω specification ties gm and R​F together; one cannot be changed without readjusting the other.

Noise figure

For the circuit of Fig.-1, neglecting flicker noise and using the usual MOS coefficients
( γ ≃ 2/3 for channel thermal noise and δ ≃ 2 for drain-to-bulk noise), the noise factor can be written to first order as

          F = 1 + γ /(gm Rs) + Rs /R​F + δ gds Rs            (2)

where Rs = 50 Ω.  
Substituting the matching condition gm = 1/Rs into (2) gives

          F = 1 + γ + Rs /R​F + δ gds Rs                    (3)

Observations from (3)  

1. The contribution γ is now a constant ( γ ≃ 0.67 ⇒ 1.6 dB ) once 50 Ω matching is enforced.  
   It cannot be improved unless a device with a smaller γ (longer channel, lower VOV, cooled
   operation, etc.) is used.

2. The term δ gds Rs is normally a few hundredths of a decibel because gds is of the order of tens of µS while Rs = 50 Ω.

3. The only term that can still be influenced by the designer is Rs /R​F.  
   It becomes negligible if R​F is made much larger than 50 Ω (e.g. ≥ 500 Ω).

Design recipe for minimum NF with Rin = 50 Ω

Step-1   Size and bias M1 so that gm ≃ 20 mS (eq.-1).  
          That automatically provides the 50 Ω match.

Step-2   Choose R​F as large as the stability / gain / bandwidth constraints allow.  
          With R​F ≥ 500–1000 Ω the term Rs /R​F falls below 0.05–0.1 dB.

Step-3   Keep M2 (the PMOS load) as small as possible and/or cascode it so that its
          noise and parasitic capacitances do not add appreciably to F and do not
          disturb the wide-band match.

Result

With the above choices the last two terms in (3) are almost zero and the lowest
achievable noise factor is

          Fmin ≈ 1 + γ  →  NFmin ≈ 10·log10(1 + γ) ≈ 2.0–2.3 dB   (γ ≃ 0.6–0.7).

Therefore, once the 50 Ω input resistance is mandatory, the NF of a simple shunt-feedback common-source stage can be pushed only down to about 2 dB by

• providing exactly gm = 1/50 Ω, and  
• making R​F as large as practical so that its own thermal noise is negligible.

## 🎯 Goal: Minimize Noise Figure (NF) while keeping Rin = 50 Ω

For a MOSFET amplifier, the dominant noise sources are:

The input impedance of a common source amplifier with a feedback resistor $R_F$ connected from the output to the input is given by the Miller effect / shunt-shunt feedback equation:
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + g_{m1} R_{out}}$$

If the loop gain ($g_{m1} R_{out}$) is high (which is typical for this amplifier to get significant gain), the input impedance simplifies to:
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}}$$
*(Note: Even if $R_F$ is the dominant output resistance, $R_{in} \approx R_F / (g_{m1} R_F) = 1/g_{m1}$. If $R_F$ is very large, $R_{in} \approx R_F / (1 + g_{m1} r_o)$. In both cases for high gain, the dominant term driving the low impedance is the transconductance).*

To maintain $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$, we must set the transconductance of the input transistor $M_1$ to:
$$g_{m1} \approx \frac{1}{R_{in}} = \frac{1}{50 \, \Omega} = 20 \, \text{mS}$$

### 2. Noise Factor Optimization
The Noise Factor ($F$) is the ratio of output SNR to input SNR. The primary noise sources in this circuit are:
1.  **Thermal noise of the feedback resistor $R_F$**: $\overline{i_{n,R_F}^2} = \frac{4kT}{R_F}$.
2.  **Channel thermal noise of $M_1$**: $\overline{i_{n,M1}^2} = 4kT \gamma g_{m1}$.
3.  **Channel thermal noise of the load $M_2$**: $\overline{i_{n,M2}^2} = 4kT \gamma g_{m2}$.

The approximate Noise Factor for this topology is:
$$F \approx 1 + \frac{R_S}{R_F} + \frac{\gamma (g_{m1} + g_{m2})}{g_{m1}^2 R_S} \dots$$
*(Simplified, the resistor noise contribution is roughly proportional to $R_S/R_F$, and the transistor noise depends on the ratio of their transconductances).*

**Optimization Strategy:**

1.  **Maximize $R_F$**:

    *   *Constraint:* $R_F$ must be large enough to ensure the input matching condition holds (i.e., $g_{m1} R_F \gg 1$). Since we set $g_{m1} = 20 \, \text{mS}$, we need $R_F \gg 50 \, \Omega$. Ideally, $R_F$ should be significantly larger than $R_S$ (e.g., $k\Omega$ range) to suppress its noise.

2.  **Transistor Sizing ($M_1$ vs $M_2$)**:
    The noise contribution from the load transistor $M_2$ appears at the output and is referred back to the input. To minimize this, we need to minimize the term $\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}$.

### 1. Circuit Analysis
The circuit shown is a **Common-Source (CS) amplifier with shunt-shunt feedback** (also known as a transimpedance amplifier configuration).
*   **$M_1$**: The input NMOS transistor in a common-source configuration.
*   **$M_2$**: A PMOS transistor connected as a diode-loaded current source (gate connected to drain). Its small-signal resistance looking into the drain is approximately $1/g_{m2}$.
*   **$R_F$**: The feedback resistor connecting the output (drain) to the input (gate).
*   **$C_1$**: A coupling capacitor (open circuit at DC, short circuit at signal frequencies).

### 2. Input Resistance ($R_{in}$)
For a shunt-shunt feedback amplifier, the input resistance is reduced by the feedback factor. The approximate expression for the input resistance looking into the gate node (excluding $C_1$) is:
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + A_v}$$
where $A_v$ is the open-loop voltage gain of the CS stage.
The gain $A_v$ is approximately $-g_{m1} R_{load}$. Here, the load is the diode-connected $M_2$, so $R_{load} \approx 1/g_{m2}$.
$$A_v \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}$$

Substituting this into the $R_{in}$ equation:
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}}$$

Given the constraint $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$, we have:
$$50 = \frac{R_F}{1 + \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}} \implies R_F = 50 \left( 1 + \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \right)$$

### 3. Noise Analysis
The main noise sources in this circuit that affect the Noise Figure (NF) are:
1.  **Thermal noise of the feedback resistor $R_F$**: The noise current is $i_{n, RF}^2 = \frac{4kT}{R_F}$. This noise is injected at the input node.
2.  **Channel thermal noise of transistor $M_1$**: The noise current is $i_{n, M1}^2 = 4kT \gamma g_{m1}$ (where $\gamma \approx 2/3$ for long-channel devices).
3.  **Noise of the load $M_2$**: Since $M_2$ is at the output, its noise is referred to the input divided by the gain squared ($A_v^2$). If $g_{m1} \gg g_{m2}$, this contribution is small.

### 4. Optimization Strategy
The goal is to minimize the Noise Figure (NF). NF is essentially the ratio of the output noise to the noise that would be present if the amplifier were noiseless. To minimize NF, we want to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio at the input.

*   **Minimize $R_F$ noise**: The noise contribution from the feedback resistor is inversely proportional to $R_F$ ($\propto 1/R_F$). Therefore, we want **$R_F$ to be as large as possible**.
*   **Maintain $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$**: From the equation $R_F = 50 (1 + g_{m1}/g_{m2})$, to increase $R_F$ while keeping $R_{in}$ constant at $50 \, \Omega$, we must **increase the ratio $(1 + g_{m1}/g_{m2})$**.

This leads to the following optimization steps:

1.  **Increase the ratio $g_{m1}/g_{m2}$**:
    *   **Increase $g_{m1}$**: Increase the transconductance of the input transistor $M_1$ (by increasing its width $W$ or bias current $I_D$). This increases the amplifier gain ($A_v \approx g_{m1}/g_{m2}$). A higher gain allows $R_F$ to be larger for the same input impedance match.
    *   **Decrease $g_{m2}$**: Decrease the transconductance of the load transistor $M_2$ (by decreasing its width or bias current). This increases the load resistance ($1/g_{m2}$) and further increases the gain.

2.  **Trade-off (The Balance)**:
    *   While increasing $g_{m1}$ allows for a larger $R_F$ (reducing $R_F$ noise), it also **increases the channel noise of $M_1$** ($4kT \gamma g_{m1}$).
    *   Therefore, you cannot just increase $g_{m1}$ indefinitely. There is an optimal point where the reduction in feedback resistor noise balances the increase in transistor $M_1$ noise.

### Conclusion
To optimize the circuit for NF:
**You should increase the ratio $g_{m1}/g_{m2}$ (i.e., make $M_1$ much stronger than $M_2$).**

This allows the feedback resistor $R_F$ to be larger (since $R_F = 50(1 + g_{m1}/g_{m2})$), which significantly reduces the thermal noise contribution from $R_F$. The optimal design point is found by balancing this benefit against the increased thermal noise generated by the larger $g_{m1}$ of transistor $M_1$. This shows that for a fixed $R_{in}$, a larger loop gain ($g_{m1} R_{out}$) requires a larger feedback resistor $R_F$.

### 2. Noise Figure (NF) Analysis
The noise figure for this resistive feedback topology is dominated by the thermal noise of the source resistance ($R_S = 50 \, \Omega$), the feedback resistor ($R_F$), and the channel thermal noise of the transistor $M_1$. The approximate expression for the Noise Figure is:
$$NF \approx 1 + \frac{R_{in}}{R_F} + \frac{R_{in} \cdot \gamma}{g_{m1} R_F^2}$$
where $\gamma$ is the noise coefficient (typically $2/3$ for long channel, $\approx 1$ for short channel).

Substituting $R_{in} = 50$ and $R_F = 50 g_{m1} R_{out}$:
$$NF \approx 1 + \frac{50}{50 g_{m1} R_{out}} + \frac{50 \gamma}{g_{m1} (50 g_{m1} R_{out})^2}$$
$$NF \approx 1 + \frac{1}{g_{m1} R_{out}} + \frac{\gamma}{50 g_{m1} (g_{m1} R_{out})^2}$$

$$NF \approx 1 + \frac{1}{A_0} + \frac{\gamma}{50 g_{m1} A_0^2}$$

### 3. Optimization Strategy
To minimize the NF, we need to **maximize the terms in the denominator**, specifically the loop gain $A_0 = g_{m1} R_{out}$ and the transconductance $g_{m1}$.

To optimize the Noise Figure (NF) of the circuit while maintaining an input resistance $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$, we need to analyze the input impedance and the noise sources of the resistive feedback amplifier (specifically, a CMOS inverter with shunt-shunt feedback).

**1. Input Impedance Analysis**
The circuit is a voltage amplifier with a feedback resistor $R_F$. The input impedance looking into the gate node (after the capacitor $C_1$) is determined by the Miller effect of the feedback resistor.
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + |A_v|}$$
where $A_v$ is the open-loop voltage gain of the CMOS inverter stage.
The gain is approximately:
$$|A_v| \approx (g_{m1} + g_{m2}) \cdot R_{out}$$
where $g_{m1}, g_{m2}$ are the transconductances of $M_1$ and $M_2$, and $R_{out} = r_{o1} || r_{o2}$ is the output resistance at the drain node.

Given the constraint $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$:
$$50 = \frac{R_F}{1 + (g_{m1} + g_{m2})R_{out}}$$
This implies that for a fixed $R_{in}$, if we increase $R_F$, we must proportionally increase the loop gain $(g_{m1} + g_{m2})R_{out}$.

**2. Noise Figure Analysis**
The main noise sources contributing to the NF are:
*   **Thermal noise of the feedback resistor $R_F$:** The noise current spectral density is $4kT/R_F$. Referred to the input, this noise contribution is inversely proportional to $R_F$. To minimize this, **$R_F$ should be as large as possible**.
*   **Channel thermal noise of transistors $M_1$ and $M_2$:** The noise current spectral density is roughly $4kT\gamma(g_{m1} + g_{m2})$. The noise figure contribution from the transistors is inversely proportional to the total transconductance $(g_{m1} + g_{m2})$. To minimize this, **$g_{m1} + g_{m2}$ should be as large as possible**.

**3. Optimization Strategy**
Combining the impedance constraint and the noise minimization goals:

*   **Maximize $R_F$:** A larger feedback resistor reduces the thermal noise injected by the resistor itself.
*   **Maximize Gain ($A_v$):** To keep $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$ while increasing $R_F$, the gain $|A_v| \approx (g_{m1} + g_{m2})R_{out}$ must increase.
*   **Maximize Transconductance ($g_m$):** Increasing $g_{m1} + g_{m2}$ helps satisfy the gain requirement and directly reduces the transistor noise contribution to the NF. This can be done by increasing the bias current or increasing the transistor widths ($W$).
*   **Maximize Output Resistance ($R_{out}$):** Increasing the output resistance (by using longer channel lengths $L$ for $M_1$ and $M_2$) increases the gain. This allows you to use a larger $R_F$ for a given $g_m$, or achieve the required gain with less $g_m$ (saving power).

**Summary of Steps to Optimize NF:**
1.  **Choose the largest possible feedback resistor $R_F$** to minimize its thermal noise contribution.
2.  **Increase the transconductance ($g_{m1} + g_{m2}$)** by sizing the transistors wider or increasing the bias current. This reduces the transistor channel noise.
3.  **Increase the output resistance ($r_{o1}, r_{o2}$)** by using longer channel lengths for the transistors. This increases the open-loop gain, which is necessary to maintain the $50 \, \Omega$ input match when using a large $R_F$.

Ideally, you want to maximize the intrinsic gain ($g_m r_o$) of the transistors. This allows $R_F$ to be very large (minimizing resistor noise) while the high $g_m$ minimizes the transistor noise, all while satisfying $R_{in} = R_F / (1 + g_m r_o) = 50 \, \Omega$. In the limit where $R_F \to \infty$ and $g_m \to \infty$ (with their ratio fixed by the impedance match), the NF approaches 0 dB (theoretical minimum).

To optimize the Noise Figure (NF) of the circuit shown (a resistive feedback amplifier using a CMOS inverter configuration) while maintaining an input resistance $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$, we need to analyze the input impedance and noise contributions of the components.

### 1. Analysis of Input Impedance ($R_{in}$)
This circuit is a shunt-shunt feedback amplifier. The input impedance looking into the node after $C_1$ is approximately given by:
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + |A_v|}$$
where $A_v$ is the open-loop voltage gain of the CMOS inverter stage.
The gain $A_v$ is approximately:
$$A_v \approx -(g_{m1} + g_{m2}) (r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2} \parallel R_F)$$
Assuming the loop gain is high ($|A_v| \gg 1$) and $R_F$ is large compared to the output impedance, the input impedance simplifies to:
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m1} + g_{m2}}$$

**Constraint:** To match $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$, we must set the total transconductance:
$$g_{m1} + g_{m2} = \frac{1}{50 \, \Omega} = 20 \, \text{mS}$$

### 2. Analysis of Noise Figure (NF)
The total Noise Figure is determined by the noise contributions of the transistors ($M_1, M_2$) and the feedback resistor ($R_F$).
*   **Transistor Noise:** The input-referred noise voltage squared due to the transistors is $\overline{V_{n,M}^2} \approx \frac{4kT\gamma}{g_{m1} + g_{m2}}$. Since $g_{m1} + g_{m2} = 1/R_{in} = 1/R_S$ (where $R_S=50\Omega$ is the source resistance), the noise factor contribution from the transistors is roughly $\gamma$ (the channel noise coefficient).
*   **Resistor Noise:** The feedback resistor $R_F$ contributes thermal noise. Its contribution to the Noise Figure is inversely proportional to $R_F$ (approximately $\frac{R_S}{R_F}$).

The approximate Noise Figure is:
$$NF \approx 1 + \gamma + \frac{R_S}{R_F}$$

### 3. Optimization Steps
To minimize the NF, we must minimize $\gamma$ and the term $\frac{R_S}{R_F}$.

**Step 1: Maximize $R_F$**
*   To minimize the noise contribution from the feedback resistor, **$R_F$ should be as large as possible**.
*   However, we must maintain $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$. From the equation $R_{in} \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + |A_v|}$, if we increase $R_F$, we must proportionally increase the gain $|A_v|$.

**Step 2: Maximize Voltage Gain ($|A_v|$) via Output Impedance**
*   Since $g_{m1} + g_{m2}$ is fixed at 20 mS, the only way to increase gain $|A_v| \approx (g_{m1} + g_{m2})R_{out}$ is to increase the output resistance $R_{out} = r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}$.
*   **Use long channel lengths ($L$) for $M_1$ and $M_2$.** The output resistance $r_o$ is proportional to channel length ($r_o \propto L$). Long channels will provide the high gain needed to support a large $R_F$.

**Step 3: Minimize Channel Noise Coefficient ($\gamma$)**
*   The parameter $\gamma$ represents excess thermal noise in the channel. For long-channel devices, $\gamma \approx 2/3$. For short-channel devices, $\gamma$ can be much larger (2 to 4).
*   **Use long channel lengths ($L$) for $M_1$ and $M_2$** to keep $\gamma$ close to the theoretical minimum of 2/3.

**Step 4: Transistor Sizing ($W/L$)**
*   You need to achieve $g_{m1} + g_{m2} = 20$ mS.
*   Since $M_2$ is a PMOS device, it has lower mobility ($\mu_p < \mu_n$) than the NMOS $M_1$. To contribute equally to the transconductance (or to balance the design), $M_2$ typically needs a larger width ($W_2 > W_1$).
*   Adjust the bias current $I_D$ and widths $W$ to achieve the target $g_m$ while keeping the devices in saturation.

### Summary
To optimize for NF with $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$:
1.  Set **$g_{m1} + g_{m2} = 20$ mS**.
2.  Use **long channel lengths** for both transistors to minimize $\gamma$ and maximize output resistance $r_o$.
3.  Choose **$R_F$ as large as possible**. The high output resistance from the long channels will allow for high gain, which keeps $R_{in}$ at 50 $\Omega$ even with a large $R_F$, thereby minimizing the resistor's noise contribution.

For an inverting amplifier with open-loop voltage gain $A_v$ (where $A_v$ is negative, so let's use magnitude $|A_v|$), the input resistance is approximately:
$$R_{in} \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + |A_v|}$$
The open-loop gain $|A_v|$ is given by the total transconductance ($G_m = g_{m1} + g_{m2}$) multiplied by the output resistance ($R_{out} = r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}$):
$$|A_v| \approx (g_{m1} + g_{m2})(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})$$

Given the constraint **$R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$**, we have:
$$50 \approx \frac{R_F}{1 + |A_v|} \implies R_F \approx 50(1 + |A_v|)$$
This tells us that to maintain a $50 \, \Omega$ input match, the feedback resistor $R_F$ must be proportional to the amplifier's gain.

**2. Analysis of Noise Figure (NF)**
The main noise sources in this circuit are:
*   Thermal noise of the source resistance ($R_S = 50 \, \Omega$).
*   Thermal noise of the feedback resistor $R_F$.
*   Channel thermal noise of transistors $M_1$ and $M_2$.

The Noise Figure ($F$) can be approximated as:
$$NF \approx 1 + \frac{4 R_S}{R_F} + \frac{\gamma}{g_{m,total} R_S}$$
*(Note: This is a simplified expression assuming high gain, where the noise of $R_F$ is the dominant resistor noise and $\gamma$ is the transistor noise coefficient).*

**3. Optimization Strategy**
Substitute the expression for $R_F$ ($R_F \approx 50 |A_v|$) into the NF equation (assuming $|A_v| \gg 1$):
$$NF \approx 1 + \frac{4 R_S}{50 |A_v|} + \frac{\gamma}{(g_{m1} + g_{m2}) R_S}$$
Since $R_S = 50 \, \Omega$:
$$NF \approx 1 + \frac{4}{|A_v|} + \frac{\gamma}{50 (g_{m1} + g_{m2})}$$

To minimize the NF, we need to minimize the added noise terms. This leads to two main conclusions:

1.  **Maximize the Open-Loop Gain ($|A_v|$):**
    *   Looking at the term $\frac{4}{|A_v|}$, increasing the gain reduces the noise contribution of the feedback resistor $R_F$.

2.  **Maximize the Transconductance ($g_{m1} + g_{m2}$):**
    *   Looking at the term $\frac{\gamma}{50 (g_{m1} + g_{m2})}$, increasing the total transconductance reduces the noise contribution of the transistors.

**Practical Steps to Optimize:**
*   **Increase Channel Length ($L$):** Use longer channel lengths for $M_1$ and $M_2$. This increases the output resistance ($r_{o1}, r_{o2}$), which significantly boosts the open-loop gain $|A_v|$. This allows you to increase $R_F$ while keeping $R_{in} = 50 \, \Omega$, suppressing the noise from the feedback resistor.
*   **Increase Transistor Width ($W$):** Increase the width of $M_1$ and $M_2$ to increase $g_m$. This directly reduces the transistor channel noise.
*   **Increase $R_F$:** As a result of increasing the gain (via $L$ and $W$), you must increase the value of $R_F$ proportionally to maintain the $50 \, \Omega$ input match.

**Summary:**
To optimize the NF, you should **maximize the gain of the core inverter stage ($M_1, M_2$)** by using long-channel devices (high $r_o$) and sufficient width (high $g_m$). ## 1. What the input node "sees"

AC‑ground the $V_{DD}$ and ground rails and label the gate node (left of $R_F$) $v_g$ and the drain node (right of $R_F$) $v_d$. Drive the gate node with a test current $i_t$ (the $R_{in}$ arrow). The gates draw no current, so the only path out of the gate node is $R_F$:

$$i_t=\frac{v_g-v_d}{R_F}$$

The drain node is a high‑impedance output (no load drawn), so the current that $R_F$ feeds into it must be absorbed by the two transistors. Both have $v_{gs}=v_g$ (M1 source at 0, M2 source at $V_{DD}$ = AC ground), hence

$$\frac{v_g-v_d}{R_F}=g_{m1}v_g+g_{m2}v_g=g\,v_g,\qquad g\triangleq g_{m1}+g_{m2}$$

Therefore $i_t=g\,v_g$ and

$$\boxed{R_{in}=\frac{v_g}{i_t}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}$$

**Key point:** $R_{in}$ depends *only* on the sum of the transconductances, **not on $R_F$**. So the matching condition

$$R_{in}=50\ \Omega \;\Rightarrow\; g_{m1}+g_{m2}=\frac{1}{50}=20\ \text{mS}$$

pins down $g$, and **$R_F$ is a free variable** that you may use purely to optimise the noise (and the gain). You cannot "trade" $R_F$ against $g$ to keep $R_{in}=50$ – that degree of freedom does not exist.

## 2. Noise figure

The internal noise has two sources: the channel (thermal) noise $4\gamma kT\,g$ of the parallel pair (effective $\gamma_{eff}=(\gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2})/(g_{m1}+g_{m2})$) and the thermal noise $4kT/R_F$ of the feedback resistor. Referring both to the *source* (the stage gain from $v_s$ to $v_d$ is $A_s=(1-gR_F)/(1+gR_s)$) gives

$$F=1+\frac{(1+gR_s)^2}{R_s(1-gR_F)^2}\Big[\gamma_{eff}\,g\,(R_F+R_s)^2+R_F\Big]$$

With the matching constraint $gR_s=1$ this becomes

$$F=1+\frac{4}{(1-gR_F)^2}\left[\frac{\gamma_{eff}(R_F+R_s)^2}{R_s}+\frac{R_F}{R_s}\right]$$

Two observations:

* The term $\dfrac{4\,\gamma_{eff}(R_F+R_s)^2/R_s}{(1-gR_F)^2}$ is the **channel‑noise** contribution; the factor $4=(1+gR_s)^2$ is the unavoidable penalty of matching a $1/g$ input to $50\ \Omega$ through gate–drain feedback (the source halves the signal at the gate).
* The term $\dfrac{4\,R_F/R_s}{(1-gR_F)^2}$ is the **$R_F$ thermal‑noise** contribution.

Both terms approach their minimum as $R_F$ is pushed to its extremes, and $F$ has a maximum (→∞) at $R_F=1/g=50\ \Omega$ (zero gain). Hence, over the usable range, the noise‑figure floor is reached for **large $R_F$**, where $R_F$'s own thermal noise is divided away by the high gain:

$$\boxed{F_{min}=1+4\,\gamma_{eff}}$$

## 3. Optimisation (with $R_{in}=50\ \Omega$ held)

You have three levers; the constraint fixes only $g_{m1}+g_{m2}=20$ mS.

1. **Allocation of $g_m$ between M1 and M2.** Because only the sum is fixed, minimise $\gamma_{eff}=(\gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2})/g$. This is linear in the split, so the optimum is to put **all of the 20 mS into the transistor with the smaller $\gamma$** (longer channel / better device) and bias the other off. If $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$, the split is irrelevant to NF – take $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=10$ mS for symmetric headroom and linearity.

2. **Value of $R_F$.** Make $R_F$ **as large as stability and the required voltage gain allow**. A large $R_F$ (i) does not change $R_{in}$, (ii) gives the stage its gain, and (iii) drives the $R_F$ thermal‑noise term to zero, so $F\to1+4\gamma_{eff}$. $R_F$ must stay finite and below the stability limit (the gate–drain feedback path), and it must keep the DC operating point valid – but since no DC gate current flows, $R_F$ can be very large without disturbing the bias.

3. **Device $\gamma$.** Reduce $\gamma_{eff}$ by using longer‑channel devices for the biased transistor.

**Resulting minimum noise figure** (with the $50\ \Omega$ match):

$$F_{min}=1+4\,\gamma_{min}\;\approx\;1+4\!\cdot\!\tfrac{2}{3}\approx 3.7\quad(\approx 5.6\ \text{dB for long‑channel devices})$$

> Note on convention: if your course refers the noise to the *gate* node rather than to the source, the source‑divider factor $(1+gR_s)^2=4$ does not appear and the floor reads $F_{min}=1+\gamma_{min}$. The optimisation conclusions (fix $g_{m1}+g_{m2}=20$ mS, allocate $g_m$ to the lower‑$\gamma$ device, maximise $R_F$ within the stability limit) are identical either way.

**In short:** hold $g_{m1}+g_{m2}=20$ mS to keep $R_{in}=50\ \Omega$; bias that $g_m$ into the lower‑$\gamma$ device; and set $R_F$ as large as stability permits. $R_F$ is your gain/knob, not your matching element.

It recognizes the inverter LNA and relevant noise sources, but its central optimization conclusion is wrong.

## What the circuit really is

After $C_1$ the input node drives the **gates of both $M_1$ and $M_2$**, and $R_F$ ties that node to the **drains of both** devices. $M_1$ (NMOS, source at gnd) and $M_2$ (PMOS, source at $V_{DD}$) are therefore two common‑source amplifiers in parallel, with their gates tied together and their drains tied together. The whole stage is equivalent to a *single* CS amplifier with

$$g_m = g_{m1}+g_{m2},\qquad r_o = r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2},\qquad v_{n,ch}^2 = 4kT(\gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2})$$

plus a gate‑to‑drain (shunt‑shunt) feedback resistor $R_F$. $M_2$ is not redundant: because the gate node draws no DC current, the DC voltage at the input node equals the DC drain voltage (diode‑like self‑bias), and $M_2$ is the only DC path that can feed the drain node from $V_{DD}$, so it supplies the bias current that $M_1$ sinks.

## What the 50 Ω constraint does to the bias

Looking into the input node (the arrow $R_{in}$) gives

$$R_{in}=\frac{R_F+r_o}{1+g_m r_o}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{g_m}\left(1+\frac{R_F}{r_o}\right)\;\approx\;\frac{1}{g_m}$$

so the matching condition **pins the total transconductance**:

$$g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{50\ \Omega}=20\ \text{mA/V}$$

This is the crucial point: *you cannot change the bias current to reduce the $1/g_m$ noise – the 50 Ω requirement locks $g_m$.* (If $R_F$ is not $\ll r_o$, then $g_m=(R_F+r_o-50)/(50\,r_o)$, i.e. increasing $R_F$ forces a *larger* $g_m$ to keep $R_{in}=50$.)

## The noise floor set by that constraint

Referred to the input node, the channel thermal noise of the parallel pair is

$$v_{n,ch,in}^2=\frac{4kT(\gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2})}{(g_{m1}+g_{m2})^2}\;\approx\;\frac{4kT\,\gamma}{g_m}$$

(the load $R_F\parallel r_o$ cancels). With $g_m\simeq 1/R_{in}$ this becomes $4kT\,\gamma\,R_{in}$, so the **thermal noise‑figure floor is**

$$NF_{th,\min}=1+\gamma \;\approx\; 2.5\;(4\ \text{dB})\quad(\gamma=1.5),\qquad 1.67\;(2.2\ \text{dB})\quad(\gamma=\tfrac23)$$

*independent of $R_F$ and $r_o$.* Every other noise term and every mismatch only **adds** to this floor. Hence "optimising for NF with $R_{in}=50$ Ω" means: keep $g_m$ at the value that gives 50 Ω, and then drive all the *extra* terms toward zero.

## The optimisation levers (and the rules)

1. **Make $R_F$ as large as the band‑width / offset budget allows.**
   - The input‑referred noise of $R_F$ is $\approx 4kT\,R_F\left(\dfrac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_F+Z_{out}}\right)^2$, which falls as $1/R_F$ for large $R_F$.
   - A large $R_F$ also pushes $g_m$ up (via the $R_{in}$ equation), which *lowers* the $4kT\gamma/g_m$ term.
   - So NF is a monotonic decreasing function of $R_F$; stop only when the input pole ($R_F$ vs. $C_{gs}$), the offset voltage ($\Delta V_{gs}$ of the matched pair), or power becomes unacceptable.

2. **Use long‑channel, low‑overdrive devices for $M_1$ and $M_2$.**
   - Large $r_o$ keeps $R_F/r_o\to0$, so the $R_{in}$ equation is not distorted and the $r_o$‑related noise term vanishes.
   - Large $WL$ at fixed $g_m$ minimises the $1/f$ gate noise $\propto 1/(C_{ox}WL)$.

3. **Choose the $M_1/M_2$ split (the self‑bias point $V_X$, i.e. the $W/L$ ratios) to minimise the extra terms.**
   Both devices carry the same DC current, so $g_{mi}=2I_D/V_{od,i}$. The combined $1/f$ and the $\gamma$‑weighted channel noise $\propto(\gamma_1/g_{m1}+\gamma_2/g_{m2})/(\dots)$ are minimised by allocating transconductance toward the device with the **smaller $\gamma$ and smaller $1/f$ coefficient** (in many processes the NMOS), while keeping both in saturation and giving $M_2$ just enough overdrive to supply the bias current.

4. **Tune $C_1$ to cancel the reactive part** of the input impedance at the centre frequency, $C_1 = 1/(\omega_0 C_{in})$ with $C_{in}=C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd}\dots$, so the input is a *pure* 50 Ω (this removes the matching‑loss term in NF and keeps the conjugate match at the band centre).

## Summary of the procedure

1. Fix $g_{m1}+g_{m2}\approx 20$ mA/V (this is non‑negotiable – it *is* the 50 Ω). Accept the $\approx 1+\gamma$ thermal floor.
2. Pick long‑channel $M_1,M_2$ (large $r_o$, low $1/f$) and size them so the self‑bias point gives the required $g_m$ and the best $1/f$/$\gamma$ split.
3. Choose $R_F$ as large as band‑width/offset permit, to push $R_F$'s own referred noise and the residual $r_o$ term to zero and to nudge $g_m$ slightly higher.
4. Set $C_1 = 1/(\omega_0 C_{in})$ for a real 50 Ω at the centre frequency.

The result is an NF as close as possible to the $1+\gamma$ (≈ 4 dB for a short‑channel device) floor that the 50 Ω constraint imposes; no choice of bias can do better, and the only thing the design can do is eliminate the *additional* noise contributed by $R_F$, $r_o$, $1/f$, and the reactive mismatch.

## What the circuit is

After $C_1$ the two transistors are wired in **parallel** (both gates to the input node, both drains to the output node), so they behave as one composite device with

$$g_m = g_{m1}+g_{m2},\qquad r_o = r_{o1}\Vert r_{o2},\qquad \gamma_{eq} g_m = \gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2}$$

The PMOS source is at $V_{DD}$ (a.c. ground) and the NMOS source is at ground, so the pair is a **common‑source** stage whose drain is fed back to its gate by $R_F$. $R_F$ therefore does two jobs: it sets the self‑bias (at d.c. $V_G=V_D$ and $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$, no extra bias network needed) and it sets the input resistance.

## Input resistance and the matching condition

Solving the two‑node small‑signal model (gate node $v$, drain node $v_o$) gives

$$R_{in}=\frac{r_o+R_F}{1+g_m r_o}$$

(For $R_F\to\infty$ this $\to\infty$, i.e. the open gate; for $R_F\to0$ it $\to1/g_m$, i.e. a diode‑connected device – both limits check out.) The 50 Ω requirement is therefore the constraint

$$\boxed{\;\frac{r_o+R_F}{1+g_m r_o}=50\;\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R_F = 50 + 50\,g_m r_o - r_o\;}$$

Note that $R_F$ and $g_m$ are **not independent**: once $r_o$ (device length + bias family) is chosen, raising $g_m$ forces $R_F$ to change if the match is to be kept at 50 Ω. (In the common textbook approximation $R_{in}\simeq R_F$, this simply means “set $R_F=50\ \Omega$ and treat $g_m$ as the free variable.”)

## Noise figure

Referring the three white‑noise sources (channel noise of $M_1$, of $M_2$, and the thermal noise of $R_F$) to the input terminal, with a 50 Ω source, the $r_o$ dependence cancels and one obtains

$$\boxed{\;NF = 1 + \frac{4R_F}{50}\,\frac{1+\gamma_{eq}\,g_m R_F}{\left(1-g_m R_F\right)^2}\;}$$

i.e. $NF$ is set by two terms: the **channel noise** of the pair (proportional to $\gamma_{eq}g_m$) and the **thermal noise of $R_F$**.

## How to optimise NF with $R_{in}=50\ \Omega$

Substituting the matching relation into the $NF$ expression shows that, for a given device technology, **both** noise terms fall as the transconductance is increased: the channel term scales $\sim 1/g_m$, and although $R_F$ grows with $g_m$, the loop gain also grows so that the $R_F$‑noise referred to the input scales $\sim 1/g_m^3$. Hence $NF$ is monotonic – there is no interior minimum in $g_m$ – and the optimum sits at the **largest feasible transconductance**, limited only by secondary constraints. Concretely:

1. **Maximise the bias current** of the pair (maximise $g_m = g_{m1}+g_{m2}$) while keeping both $M_1$ and $M_2$ in saturation and within the power budget. This is the dominant NF lever.
2. **Set $R_F$ from the match equation** above, not by eye. Do not force $R_F=50\ \Omega$ unless $g_m r_o\ll1$; otherwise the real part of $R_{in}$ will drift off 50 Ω.
3. **Choose the $M_1/M_2$ split** for the smallest $\gamma_{eq}g_m$: put more $g_m$ in the device with the smaller $\gamma$ (and use longer channels / better devices for the higher‑$g_m$ device to push the $1/f$ corner down). The parallel pair also lets you place the gate bias at a comfortable mid‑rail voltage without an extra bias network.
4. **Mind the size–capacitance trade‑off.** $g_m$ can be raised either by bias current or by width $W$; widening the devices raises $C_{gs}$, which appears in parallel at the input and degrades the 50 Ω match at high frequency (the circuit has no inductor to neutralise it). So for a given operating band, pick the largest $g_m$ that still keeps $\omega C_{gs}$ small enough that the real‑part match stays at 50 Ω over the band.

**Bottom line:** with the input match tied to the feedback network, the NF is minimised by driving the composite transconductance as high as power, saturation, $1/f$ and the input‑capacitance/bandwidth limits allow, using $R_F$ only to satisfy $(r_o+R_F)/(1+g_m r_o)=50\ \Omega$, and using the $M_1/M_2$ ratio and channel lengths to minimise $\gamma_{eq}$ and the flicker corner. The residual $NF$ floor is then set by the thermal noise of the 50 Ω match element ($R_F$) and the best achievable $\gamma_{eq}$.
